question: A 28-year-old presents with a painful red eye and blurred vision. Which pattern of injection MOST suggests anterior uveitis rather than bacterial conjunctivitis?

answers.text: Diffuse conjunctival injection maximal in the fornices with mucopurulent discharge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diffuse injection maximal in the fornices with discharge is classic for bacterial conjunctivitis — a benign cause of red eye.

answers.text: Circumcorneal (ciliary) injection with deep aching pain and photophobia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Circumcorneal (pericorneal/ciliary) injection reflects deep episcleral vessel engorgement and points strongly to anterior uveitis or acute angle-closure glaucoma — both require urgent referral.

answers.text: Bright red subconjunctival haemorrhage with no pain and normal vision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Subconjunctival haemorrhage is typically painless with normal vision and is almost always benign, not a sign of intraocular inflammation.

answers.text: Follicular reaction on the tarsal conjunctiva with watery discharge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Follicular reaction with watery discharge is the hallmark of viral (adenoviral) conjunctivitis — a common but benign cause.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the danger signs in red eye: circumcorneal injection, reduced vision, severe pain, and corneal haze all indicate intraocular pathology requiring urgent referral.
Correct. Circumcorneal injection with deep pain and photophobia is a red flag — never dismiss it as conjunctivitis without ruling out uveitis or acute glaucoma.
